text: In addition to hydrocarbon waxes and oils, TOD also produced a small fraction of aqueous oils containing acids, alcohols, and ketones. The effects of plastic pre-washing were investigated by comparing the conversion of virgin plastics and unwashed PC waste plastics. Unwashed PC waste plastics produced overall lower but comparable yields of condensables than virgin plastics. For example, the condensable yields were 85.5% and 76.5% for virgin HDPE and PP, whereas the yields from PC HDPE and PP were 79% and 71%, respectively. The PC waste plastic pyrolysis produced slightly more char and gases than virgin plastics. The variations between the results are most likely due to impurities in the plastics. To confirm, pyrolysis of polyolefin plastics with 13 additives, fillers, and pigments with known concentrations was carried out in CUWP (Radhakrishnan et al., 2025). The results showed that embedded impurities affect pyrolysis by increasing the degree of dehydrogenation and the formation of carbon residues. It is observed that the impurities decompose at pyrolysis temperatures. Following pyrolysis of waste plastics in lab-scale reactors, pyrolysis of low-quality mixed plastics was also successfully conducted at Iowa State University using a pilot-scale bubbling fluidized-bed reactor. The feedstock selection for the pilot trial was a mixture of unwashed post-consumer HDPE and PP plastics. The HPDE and PP were each hand sorted from a post-consumer bale and milled to a size of 3-5 mm. The plastics were then mixed together at a mass ratio of 1:1. A picture of the unwashed mixture of post-consumer HDPE and PP used in the pilot thermal conversion is shown in Figure 3.3.1. Approximately 200 kg of the material was prepared. Figure 3.3.1. Milled post-consumer waste consisting of 50:50 mix of HDPE and PP. A schematic of the Iowa State University’s pilot-scale pyrolyzer is shown in Figure 3.3.2 (Polin et al., 2019). The pyrolyzer consists of a feedstock metering system, fluidized bed reactor, cyclones for solid removal, and a fractionation collection system for condensable products. To process plastics, the system was slightly modified from traditional biomass set-ups, such as modifications to collect temperatures. Furthermore, the pilot experiment included operation under TOD conditions and a reaction temperature of 600 °C. We successfully processed mixed post-consumer waste continuously at a feedstocks rate of up to 2.5 kg/h for a total of approximately 6 hours while keeping major contaminant levels below 500 ppm. The pyrolysis oil from this pilot scale run was shipped to Ive Hermans as a part of the Topic Area 4 team. The pilot trial was stopped due to labor constraints and therefore restricted the continuous operation to a target of 24 hours.
